title: What is OAuth2 — a framework for DELEGATED AUTHORIZATION (letting a third-party app access your resources without sharing your password) — and what are the four roles (Resource Owner, Client, Authorization Server, Resource Server)?
shortTitle: OAuth2 — Delegated Authorization and Its Four Roles

s1_definition.profdef: OAuth2 is an authorization framework that lets a third-party application obtain limited access to a user's resources on another service without the user sharing their password with that application. Instead of handing over credentials, the user authorizes the app, and the app receives a scoped, expiring access token. OAuth2 defines four roles: the Resource Owner (the user who owns the data), the Client (the app requesting access), the Authorization Server (which authenticates the owner and issues tokens), and the Resource Server (which hosts the protected resources and accepts the tokens).
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants a budgeting app to read his National Bank of India transaction history. He does NOT give the app his net-banking password. Instead the app sends him to the bank's own login page, Rajesh signs in there and approves "allow this app to READ my transactions," and the bank hands the app a limited pass that only reads transactions and expires soon. Rajesh is the Resource Owner, the budgeting app is the Client, the bank's login system is the Authorization Server, and the bank's transactions API is the Resource Server.
s1_definition.oneliner: OAuth2 lets you grant an app limited, revocable access to your data without ever giving it your password.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** OAuth2 is an authorization framework that lets a third-party application obtain limited access to a user's resources on another service without the user sharing their password with that application. Instead of handing over credentials, the user authorizes the app, and the app receives a scoped, expiring access token. OAuth2 defines four roles: the Resource Owner (the user who owns the data), the Client (the app requesting access), the Authorization Server (which authenticates the owner and issues tokens), and the Resource Server (which hosts the protected resources and accepts the tokens).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh wants a budgeting app to read his National Bank of India transaction history. He does NOT give the app his net-banking password. Instead the app sends him to the bank's own login page, Rajesh signs in there and approves "allow this app to READ my transactions," and the bank hands the app a limited pass that only reads transactions and expires soon. Rajesh is the Resource Owner, the budgeting app is the Client, the bank's login system is the Authorization Server, and the bank's transactions API is the Resource Server.

**One line to remember:** OAuth2 lets you grant an app limited, revocable access to your data without ever giving it your password.

sections.s2_technical:
The Resource Owner is the human who owns the data and can grant access. The Client is the application that wants access on the owner's behalf; it is registered with the Authorization Server and has a client_id (and usually a client_secret for confidential clients). The Authorization Server authenticates the owner, shows a consent screen, and issues tokens at its token endpoint. The Resource Server hosts the APIs and validates the access token (checking signature/introspection and scopes) before serving data.

The central idea is scoped, delegated access via tokens rather than credential sharing. The client requests specific scopes like `transactions:read`, and the issued access token encodes exactly those scopes. For example the Resource Server enforces `@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('SCOPE_transactions:read')")` on its endpoint, so the budgeting app can read but cannot transfer money. Tokens expire, so access is time-limited, and the owner can revoke consent at any time, which no shared password would allow.

The senior nuance is that OAuth2 is about authorization, not authentication — it answers "what may this client do," not "who is the user." Services that need to know the user's identity layer OpenID Connect on top, which adds an ID token. Another nuance is client confidentiality: a server-side web app is a confidential client that can protect a secret, whereas a single-page app or mobile app is a public client that cannot, which changes which flow and protections you use (PKCE). Correctly separating the four roles is what keeps the user's password out of the third-party app entirely.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A budgeting startup wants to show Rajesh his spending from National Bank of India. The naive approach is to ask Rajesh for his net-banking password, which is catastrophic: the app could do anything, forever, and the password is now exposed. This is exactly the problem OAuth2 solves — delegated access without password sharing.

Problem 2 — The bank must make sure the app can only READ transactions, not move money, and only for a limited time. This is exactly why the four roles and scoped tokens exist — the Authorization Server issues a token limited to transactions:read, and the Resource Server enforces that scope.

Our mini-project models the four roles as classes: a `ResourceOwner`, a `Client`, an `AuthorizationServer` that issues a scoped token after consent, and a `ResourceServer` that serves data only if the token carries the right scope. The demo shows a read succeeding and a transfer being refused with the same token.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Resource Owner Rajesh, Client budgetApp, and a requested scope of transactions:read.

Step 1: The Client sends Rajesh to the Authorization Server. Rajesh authenticates there with the bank's own login and consents to transactions:read. The budgeting app never sees his password — that is the whole point of delegated authorization.

Step 2: The Authorization Server issues an AccessToken whose subject is rajesh, client is budgetapp, and scopes is exactly {transactions:read}. The token is scoped and will expire, so access is limited and revocable.

Step 3: The Client calls the Resource Server's getTransactions with the token. The Resource Server checks the token carries transactions:read, which it does, and returns the transaction list. The data flowed without the app ever holding credentials.

Step 4: The Client tries the Resource Server's transfer with the same token. The Resource Server requires transactions:write, which the token does not carry, so it throws InsufficientScopeException, mapped to HTTP 403. This shows how scopes confine a delegated token to exactly what the owner approved.

```text
2026-10-31 23:10:00.010 INFO    [OAuthRolesDemo] Auth server issued scoped token: [transactions:read]
2026-10-31 23:10:00.012 INFO    [OAuthRolesDemo] Resource server returned: [2026-10-01 -5000 groceries, 2026-10-05 -2000 fuel]
2026-10-31 23:10:00.013 SEVERE  [OAuthRolesDemo] Transfer refused: token lacks scope: transactions:write
```


sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — OAuth2 Delegated Authorization ═══

  ┌──────────────┐          ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ BudgetApp    │          │ Authorization Server│ authenticate owner,
  │ (Client)     │◀────────▶│ (bank login + token)│ consent, issue scoped token
  └──────┬───────┘          └─────────────────────┘
         │ Bearer scoped token
         ▼
  ┌─────────────────────┐   validates token + scope
  │ Resource Server     │── transactions:read  → allow
  │ (bank APIs)         │── transactions:write → deny
  └─────────────────────┘
  Resource Owner (Rajesh) logs in ONLY at the Authorization Server
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — OAuth2 Four Roles ═══

  ┌──────────────────┐  authorize(owner,client,scopes)  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ AuthorizationServer│──────────────────────────────▶ │ AccessToken       │
  │ + authorize(...)  │  issues                          │ {subject,clientId,│
  └──────────────────┘                                   │  scopes}          │
                                                         └────────┬──────────┘
  ┌──────────────────┐  getTransactions(token, acct)              │ presented to
  │ ResourceServer   │  transfer(token, from,to,amt)              ▼
  │ + requireScope() │◀──────────────────────────────── (Bearer token)
  └──────────────────┘  throws InsufficientScopeException if scope absent

  Roles:
    ResourceOwner  = user who owns the data (authenticates at Auth Server)
    Client         = third-party app (has client_id/secret)
    AuthServer     = authenticates owner + issues scoped tokens
    ResourceServer = hosts APIs, enforces scopes
  Principle of least privilege: token carries ONLY consented scopes
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
OAuth2 is an authorization framework that lets a third-party application access a user's resources on another service without the user ever sharing their password with that application. Instead of handing over credentials, the user authorizes the app at a trusted login page, and the app receives a scoped, expiring access token. The key word is delegated authorization — the user delegates limited access, not their identity or their password.

OAuth2 defines four roles, and being able to name them cleanly is what interviewers look for. The Resource Owner is the user who owns the data. The Client is the application requesting access on the user's behalf. The Authorization Server authenticates the owner, shows a consent screen, and issues tokens. The Resource Server hosts the protected APIs and validates the token and its scopes before serving data.

In my banking example a budgeting app wants to read Rajesh's transactions from National Bank of India. Rajesh logs in at the bank's own Authorization Server and consents to transactions:read only. The app receives a token limited to that scope, so when it reads transactions the Resource Server allows it, but when it tries to transfer money the Resource Server refuses because the token lacks the write scope. Rajesh never gave the app his password, and he can revoke consent at any time.

The nuance I always add is that OAuth2 is about authorization, not authentication — it says what a client may do, not who the user is. When a service also needs the user's identity, we layer OpenID Connect on top, which adds an ID token. And because a server-side app can keep a client secret but a single-page or mobile app cannot, the choice of flow and extra protections like PKCE depends on whether the client is confidential or public.

---

keyPoints: OAuth2: delegated authorization — app accesses user data on their behalf
Authorization Code Flow: safest for web apps — code exchanged server-to-server
PKCE: extra security for mobile/SPA — no client secret needed
OIDC: authentication layer on top of OAuth2 — ID token with user info
